extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on selecting and managing methods of narration in novels: scenic vs panoramic presentation, choice and handling of centre of vision/point of view, scene placement and preparation, and authorial distance. Aimed at writers planning method and structure for a novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish scenic and panoramic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between 'scenic' (immediate, dramatized scenes presenting visible and audible facts) and 'panoramic' (broad, survey-like presentation of a world or society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the scenic method when you want the reader to be present in a moment (stageable scenes, dialogue, action). Use the panoramic method for broad surveys, typical impressions, or to present a landscape of characters and manners (e.g., Thackeray's sweeping view of a society). A novel may legitimately use both, but the critic expects to find the principle on which the alternation is managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make scenes necessary and prepared
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A scene that is not really wanted, and that does nothing in particular...is a weakness in a story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place each scene where 'everything is ready for it' so the action is 'ripe' and the scene 'conclusively establishes one aspect of it and opens the view towards the next.' Avoid gratuitous scenes; ensure summary or prior development prepares the occasion so the scene can make its full effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene as primary means of starting interest
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The scene holds the place of honour, that it is the readiest means of starting an interest and raising a question.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a scene to prompt immediate speculation about the characters. Use scenes again for climaxes and resolutions; dovetail scenes and summaries so scenes reappear when they can fulfill and complete what they began.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether subject is pictorial or dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if the novel's true subject is a portrait/picture (pictorial) or a conflict/strife of wills (dramatic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the book is essentially pictorial (as argued for Madame Bovary), emphasize rendering characters and environment vividly; if dramatic, emphasize actions, suspense, and turning-points. Choose the method best suited to the irreducible idea at the heart of the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and maintain a centre of vision/point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: 'With which of the characters, if with any of them, is the writer to identify himself, which is he to “go behind”?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a central consciousness (or an external authorial stance) to command the subject. If the subject can be fully rendered from one character's perspective, confine to that point of view. Avoid haphazard or unnecessary plunges into other minds which confuse focus; shifts may occur but should be motivated and controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage shifts between subjective and objective rendering
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors will often alternate between rendering incidents as they appear in somebody's thought (subjective) and presenting the visible facts directly (objective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious when you are making a scene 'bathed in the climate' of a character's mood versus when you present direct, stageable facts. Use subjective rendering to show inner life; use objective rendering when facts themselves should tell the story. Mixing is allowable but must follow a discernible principle tied to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a consistent plan for mixing methods
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The only law that binds him throughout... is the need to be consistent on some plan, to follow the principle he has adopted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you mix dramatic, pictorial, scenic, and panoramic devices, establish and follow an underlying principle that justifies alternation. Inconsistent, arbitrary mixing weakens the work; deliberate, principled fusion creates layers and stratification of treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authorial distance/irony to enable transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a certain aloofness even when entering a character's mind so the reader is not wholly identified with that consciousness; a hint of irony prevents being lost in subjective immersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the author must shift from a character's limited vision to a wider perspective, disguise the transition by maintaining a tone of irony or measured distance. This allows the author to 'abandon her manner of looking' without creating a jarring change of values or dislocating the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide compensating perception when character's vision is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: If your protagonist has a 'poor' or narrow intelligence, the author must supply what the character cannot perceive so the world is fully known to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not keep the narrative wholly inside a mind that cannot account for the full world you wish to portray. Introduce controlled shifts or authorial commentary that reveal the wider setting, social ironies, and other characters—without bluntly rupturing the narrative stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render setting as integral and as distinct as characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the scenery and town-life with the same intensity as the heroine; setting should not be a subdued background but part of the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize place and secondary figures sharply; make the environment 'as thoroughly characterized as she is' so that setting contributes directly to the subject (e.g., Yonville in Madame Bovary). The world may act as a co-player in a drama or as essential material in a portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare secondary viewpoints for narrative closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Early episodes about secondary characters may be necessary in order to make later narrative effects (for example, Charles's youth is prepared to make his discovery at the end effective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce and develop other characters' inner lives or histories when they will be needed for the final impact or to frame the subject. Apparent digressions (e.g., biographical material) can be justified by their role in the book's framing or climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let incidents serve the author's larger purpose (illustration vs essential plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the story may 'simply illustrate' the subject rather than be indispensable plot points; the novelist chooses emphasis accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which incidents are illustrative (used to make a pictorial impression) and which are structural (drive dramatic stakes). A novelist like Flaubert allows many events to be picturesque rather than decisive; make that choice intentionally based on whether you want a picture or a drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid naked authorial intrusion that damages identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Openly changing from an immersed storyteller to an outside, critical authorial voice is disconcerting and may weaken prior experience granted to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mask necessary shifts in stance so the reader is not 'wrenched out' of identification. If an authorial commentary or omniscient judgment is required, integrate it with the established tone (e.g., irony rather than boastful assertion) to maintain coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange summary and chronicle to lead into scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'On the whole we expect to find that the scene presently yields to some kind of chronicle or summary, and that this in turn prepares the way and leads into the occasion that fulfils it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use summaries and chronicle passages to cover intervening time or to gather the story so that when a scene returns it has proper preparation and resonance. Balance scenic immediacy with summarizing moves to control pacing and focus.
